drills.title: vs Hongme (824) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: That g5 pawn is the whole issue here — your f4 bishop is hanging and needs to move. Bxf5 ignores it completely: your d3 bishop wins the trade on f5, but Black doesn't even recapture there — gxf4 just snaps off your other bishop for a single pawn, and your remaining bishop still has to scurry back to d3 once Black's e6 pawn hits f5 anyway. You end up down a full piece for nothing. Bg3 fixes the real problem by sliding the attacked bishop to safety first, keeping both bishops and the central tension alive — after h5 Bxf5 exf5 h4 you're still doing fine. Always move the piece that's actually under attack before reaching for a trade elsewhere.
drills.threat: Black's pawn on g5 is already attacking your bishop on f4, right now, before you even move.

drills.coachNote: White's d4 pawn is leaning on your e5 pawn, and if you leave that tension alone, d5 comes next and hits both your c6 knight and e6 square at once. Be6 develops a piece but does nothing about that — so White plays d5!, your bishop has to scamper to g4, and then dxc6 wins your knight for a pawn since b7 can only recapture the pawn, not the piece. That's a full knight lost for free this early. exd4 was the move: it just removes the attacker, and after Nxd4 Be7 O-O Nf6 you've got a totally normal, safe position. When a central pawn is directly attacked, resolve that tension before you develop anything else.

drills.coachNote: That queen on b3 isn't just sitting there — it's one move from a4+, and a check always comes with a free tempo. Nxe4 grabs a pawn, but after Qa4+ Qd7 Qxe4, White just takes the knight back, and now you've lost a whole knight for a pawn on top of a position that was already rough. O-O was the move: it gets your king off the e-file and out of check range entirely, so there's no intermezzo for White to exploit, and you can look for e4 again later on better terms. drills.coachNote: That knight on e5 has more squares than it looks like, and g6 is the key one — from there it hits your queen on e7 and your rook on f8 in one shot. f6 was meant to kick the knight away, but it walks straight into Ng6!: your queen has to run with Qf7, and then Nxf8 Rxf8 nets White a rook for a knight. Rfe8 was the fix — tuck the rook off f8 first, so the knight has nothing to fork, and only then is kicking it with f6 actually safe. Before you attack a piece, always check every square it can jump to first.

drills.coachNote: White's whole idea is Nxd4, because after exd4 the queen swings to g4 and hits two things at once — your newly recaptured d4 pawn and the g7 pawn. Nd4 walks right into that: Nxd4 exd4 Qg4 forces you to spend a move on Qf6 just to cover both, losing time and structure with nothing to show for it. Ne7 avoids the whole trade — it develops toward castling, keeps your center pawn where it is, and after c4 g6 Qb3 Rb8 d4 you're still solid and flexible. Don't send a piece to a square where the opponent is itching to trade and pick up a tempo right after.

drills.coachNote: The bishop on e4 and knight on f3 are just waiting for d4 to challenge your center — that e5 pawn is the backbone of your +4.2 position. Bd7 develops a piece but does nothing to stop it, so White gets d4! exd4 Nxd4, reopening the position and chewing a huge chunk out of your edge even though no material changes hands — you drop from crushing to merely better. d5 was the answer: it meets the threat head-on by gaining space and kicking the e4 bishop before White can choose the moment, and if White tries Bxh7+ anyway, Kxh7 Nxe5 Bxe5 Bxe5 just hands you more material. When you're up on space, don't let the opponent pick when to open the center — push first.

drills.coachNote: That stray bishop on a1 is a loose piece White's f1 rook is lined up to grab the moment you give White a free move. Kxf8 recaptures immediately but hands White exactly that free move: Rxa1 just wins your bishop back for nothing, knocking your edge down from +7 to around +5. Bd4+ was the move — check comes first, so White has to answer with Kh1 instead of grabbing the loose bishop, and only then do you play Kxf8 safely with the a1 bishop still intact. After Nxf4 Bf5 c3 you're still comfortably on top. Before a routine recapture, always scan for a check that buys time to save something else hanging.
drills.threat: Your bishop on a1 is sitting deep in White's camp with no defender, and White's rook on f1 can simply take it for free.

Bh4 was the fix: it steps the attacked bishop to safety while still leaning on the f6 knight and the dark squares, so after Rg8 Nbd2 Bh3 Bg3 Bg4 you keep all your initiative. drills.coachNote: White's early Qf3 is quietly aiming down the long diagonal at b7, a square you loosened with ...b6, while the e4 pawn is poised to push. Nc6 instead develops, guards e5, and keeps the knight flexible; after Nh3 h6 c3 e5 you're already comfortable. Early on, check what a pawn push attacks before committing a piece to its path.

Kf3 does the same basic job but keeps your plan intact — after Kf7 e4 Ke7 Ke3 you're still marching toward the key squares with the e-pawn break still in hand. drills.coachNote: White's pawn on g5 is the real problem — it's attacking your knight on f6, and grabbing it with hxg5 doesn't make that attacker disappear. You played hxg5, but White just recaptures hxg5 and the pawn is right back on g5 glaring at your knight; you played e5 without addressing it, so gxf6 won the knight outright, a full piece dropping your eval another 2.5 pawns.
